title: Plan a Skatepark for Your Town
bigQuestion: What does it take to turn a town's wish for a skatepark into a safe, welcoming place that gets built?

story.title: From Napkin to Council Chamber
story.kicker: A rough sketch at a diner turns into a plan that a whole town can see.
paragraphs: Lena is a night-shift nurse who started skating again at 38, after her son asked her to teach him. One morning after work, at a diner near the high school, she listens to three teenagers at the next booth. They have been chased out of a grocery store parking lot again. One of them, Andre, pulls a napkin from the holder and starts drawing a bank, a ledge and a little bowl.

Lena leans over and asks if she can add something. She draws a flat area off to one side with a small quarter pipe. 'For beginners,' she says, 'and for people like me.' Andre adds a bench for parents. Before the coffee is gone, the napkin has a parking lot, a path, a light pole and a question mark where the money should go.

Over the next two years the napkin becomes a folder. There are survey results from three schools, a list of 140 people who skate in town, and photos from a skate-a-thon that raised money for the design. A city parks planner joins the group, then a design firm that builds skateparks. At community meetings, children press sticky dots on the features they want most.

On a Tuesday night in spring, Andre stands at a microphone in the council chamber. Behind him, a screen shows a set of real drawings: a plaza section, a bowl, a beginner area with gentle banks, a smooth path from the sidewalk wide enough for a wheelchair, and lights on a timer. He has two minutes. He starts with the napkin.

The vote that night only approves the site. The design and the money will come back at later meetings, and the group will be there for each one. Walking out, Lena tells Andre that most of the work was not the drawing. It was showing up, counting people, answering every worry with a fact and keeping the whole town in the picture.
story.think: If you sketched a skatepark for your own town, who would you invite to help, and what would you draw first?

lessons.title: From Idea to Opening Day
lessons.mainIdea: Most public skateparks are built by cities after advocates show a need, the public helps design it and the council approves the money.
reading: Most public skateparks in the United States start the same way: a group of skaters and parents asks the city for a place to ride. The park is usually built by the city's parks department on public land, with money the city council approves. Between the first request and opening day there are often several years of meetings, planning and fundraising.

The usual steps run in order. First, *advocates*, the people pushing for the park, form a group and show that there is a need. Next, the city looks at possible sites and holds public meetings. Then a *design firm* draws plans and estimates the cost. After that, the city council votes to approve and fund the project, a *contractor* builds it, and the park opens with rules posted.

Many parks today are designed by firms that specialize in skateparks, often started or staffed by skaters. They know how transitions, ledges and flat ground fit together so riders do not crash into each other. Concrete is the usual choice for permanent public parks, shaped by crews who build skateparks, because forming smooth curves in wet concrete takes practice.

This process grew out of hard lessons. Many of the paid parks that opened in the late 1970s, after Carlsbad Skatepark and Skateboard City both opened in 1976, closed in the early 1980s over insurance costs. Free public parks run by cities became common later, as towns worked out *liability*, the question of who is responsible when someone gets hurt.

words.d: people who speak up and work for a cause, such as a new skatepark
a company that plans and draws a project and estimates what it will cost
a company hired to build a project from the approved plans
legal responsibility for harm, such as an injury on public property

look.title: The Path on a Wall Calendar
look.text: Picture a wall calendar covering three years. Year one: the advocates' first meeting, a survey, a skate-a-thon. Year two: site visits, three community meetings, a design firm's drawings, a cost estimate. Year three: the council vote, a construction fence going up, concrete crews shaping the bowl, and a ribbon across the gate on opening day.
look.prompt: Which step on the calendar do you think takes the longest in a town like yours, and why?

check.why: Public parks are usually built by a city's parks department on public land, with money the council approves.

choices: The council votes to approve and fund the project
check.why: A contractor builds only after the council approves the plans and the money.

check.q: Why did many paid skateparks close in the early 1980s?
choices: Wheels became too hard to ride
check.why: Many paid parks of the late 1970s closed in the early 1980s because insurance cost too much.

lessons.title: Community Meetings
lessons.mainIdea: At community meetings, skaters and neighbors shape a park's design, and worries answered with facts there are less likely to block it later.
reading: A *community meeting* is where a park's design really begins. The city or the design firm invites skaters, parents, neighbors and anyone else interested. Designers often bring large printouts of the site and let people point, draw and vote on features with sticky dots. Young skaters who are too young to vote in elections can still shape the park here.

Good meetings are planned around the people who will use the park. Holding them after school or on a weekend, near the site, lets students come. A *survey* on paper and online, offered in Spanish or other languages the town speaks, brings in people who cannot attend. Each comment is written down so the next drawing can respond to it.

Neighbors may come with worries about noise, litter, parking or crowds. Answering with facts works better than arguing: show where the nearest homes are, when the lights will switch off and who will empty the trash cans. A worry that is heard and answered at a meeting is less likely to turn into a no vote at the council later.

Most designs go through rounds. The firm presents a *concept design*, a first rough plan, and people react to it. A revised drawing comes back at the next meeting. Skaters who come to every round see their ideas, such as a lower ledge or a small bowl, appear in the plans.

words.d: a public gathering where people share ideas and concerns about a local project
a set of questions asked of many people to learn what they think or need
a first, rough plan shown to the public before the detailed drawings

look.title: Sticky Dots on the Wall
look.text: Four big boards line a school gym. One shows a street plaza, one a bowl, one a beginner area, one a flow course. Each person gets five green dots. A ten-year-old puts three on the beginner area. A grandfather who walks his dog nearby puts one on the board with trees for shade. By the end, the beginner board is crowded with green.
look.prompt: What would the dots tell the designers, and what would you want to ask the people who did not come?

check.q: What are sticky dots used for at a design meeting?
choices: Letting people vote on the features they want
check.why: Designers let people place dots on features to show what the community wants most.

check.q: How can a city get more students to its meetings?
choices: Hold them during school hours far from the site
Hold them after school or on weekends near the site
check.why: Meeting times and places that fit students' days let them come and be heard.

check.q: What is the best way to answer a neighbor's worry about noise?
choices: Argue that skaters were there first
Ignore it until the council vote
Promise there will be no sound at all
Show facts, such as where homes are and when lights switch off
check.why: Facts about distance, hours and plans answer worries better than arguing.

lessons.title: Budgets and Funding
lessons.mainIdea: A park's budget adds design and a contingency to construction, and the money usually comes from several sources at once.
reading: A skatepark's cost depends mostly on its size and its materials. Here is a worked example: a 1,200-square-meter concrete park at an example price of $500 per square meter. The construction cost is 1,200 × 500 = $600,000. Real prices vary widely by region and year, so a real budget uses local quotes from builders.

Construction is not the whole budget. Design and engineering, permits, lighting, paths, signs and a *contingency*, money held back for surprises, go on top. If design is 10% of construction and the contingency is another 10%, each adds 0.10 × 600,000 = $60,000. That brings the example to $720,000 before lights and paths.

Money usually comes from several places at once. A city's *capital budget*, its plan for long-lasting projects such as parks and roads, often pays the largest share. State park grants, local businesses, service clubs and skater fundraisers fill the gap. The Skatepark Project, founded in 2002 as the Tony Hawk Foundation and renamed in 2020, gives a *grant*, along with advice, to many communities building public parks.

Fundraising also proves support. A council member who sees teenagers running a skate-a-thon knows the park has a real community behind it. Keep a public tally of dollars raised and hours volunteered. Plan for upkeep too: concrete parks need little care beyond cleaning and patching, but someone must budget for it every year.

words.d: money set aside in a budget for problems or costs no one expected
a government's plan for paying for long-lasting projects such as parks, roads and buildings
money given for a project that does not have to be paid back

look.title: An Example Skatepark Budget
look.cite: Worked example: 1,200 m² at an example $500 per m²; other lines are example figures
look.prompt: What is the total of all four lines, and which line would you protect first if the council asked for cuts?

check.q: In the example, what does a 1,200 m² park cost to build at $500 per m²?
check.why: 1,200 × 500 = $600,000 for construction.

check.q: What is a contingency in a budget?
check.why: A contingency is money set aside for costs no one planned for.

check.q: What was The Skatepark Project called when it was founded in 2002?

lessons.title: In Front of the City Council
lessons.mainIdea: The city council decides because it controls the budget, and short, factual public comments help members say yes.
reading: The *city council*, the elected group that governs a town, makes the final decision because it controls the budget. A skatepark usually reaches the council as an item on the *agenda*, the meeting's published list of business. Often a staff report from the parks department explains the site, the design and the cost. Members of the public can usually speak during *public comment*, which is often limited to a few minutes each.

A short, clear talk works best. Say who you are and where you live, state what you are asking for, give two or three facts and thank the council. A student might say how far they now travel to skate, or that they keep getting sent away from parking lots. A parent might describe a child who found friends and exercise on a board. Bring a one-page summary to hand out.

Council members also weigh risk. Some states, including California, have laws that treat skateboarding at a public park as a *hazardous recreational activity*. Such laws limit a city's responsibility when a rider is hurt, especially when rules such as wearing a helmet are posted. Asking city staff how your state handles this answers a common worry before anyone raises it.

A decision may come in steps: first a site, then a design, then the money. Each step is another chance to show up. Steady, polite presence over months often matters more than one big night. Keep a list of which council members asked which questions, and bring an answer to each at the next meeting.

words.d: the elected group that makes laws and budget decisions for a town or city
the published list of topics a meeting will cover
the time at a public meeting when anyone may speak to the officials
a legal label some states give risky sports, which limits a city's responsibility for injuries

look.text: A timer on the wall reads 2:00. A speaker steps up: 'My name is Andre. I live on Oak Street and I'm a junior at the high school. Forty of us skate here, and right now we ride in parking lots. We are asking you to approve the site by the library. We raised $8,000 already. Thank you.' The timer still shows twenty seconds.

check.why: The council approves spending, so it decides whether the park is funded and built.

choices: The published list of topics a meeting will cover
check.why: An agenda lists the business a meeting will take up, such as a skatepark item.

choices: Require every rider to pay a fee

check.why: These laws limit a city's liability for injuries, especially when rules are posted.

lessons.title: Street Plaza or Bowl
lessons.mainIdea: A street plaza copies city features, a bowl comes from the pool tradition, and many towns mix both in a hybrid park.
reading: A *street plaza* copies the city on purpose: ledges, benches, rails, manual pads, banks and short stairs set in an open, flat space. It grew from the street era of the 1990s, when skaters filmed at real plazas and schoolyards in videos such as Blind's Video Days (1991). A plaza gives street skaters a legal place to practice what they once did on private property.

A *bowl* is a deep, rounded basin with curved walls and a metal or concrete edge along the top. Bowls come from the backyard pools skaters rode during the California drought of 1976–77. Riders carve around the walls, pump through the curves to keep their speed, and do tricks at the lip.

*Transition* is the general word for curved riding surfaces, from small quarter pipes to tall bowls. Many towns choose a *hybrid* park that mixes both styles: a street section, a bowl and smooth banks that link them. Because each area draws different riders, a hybrid spreads people out and serves more ages and styles.

The right mix depends on who will skate there. At the meetings, count skaters by the style they ride and ask where they ride now. A town full of young beginners needs low banks and wide flat ground more than a tall, deep bowl. Skaters who ride both styles can say which features they would use every week, which helps the designers rank them.

words.d: a skatepark area built like a city square, with ledges, rails, stairs and banks
a deep, rounded skatepark basin with curved walls, based on backyard pools
any curved riding surface, such as a quarter pipe or the wall of a bowl
a park that mixes street features and transition in one design

look.title: Two Corners of One Park
look.text: In one corner, a flat plaza holds a long granite ledge, a manual pad, a three-stair with a low rail and a gentle bank. Riders wait their turn, roll one line and circle back. In the other corner, a bowl dips below the ground. A rider carves around its curved wall, the coping clicking under the back truck, while two others sit on the deck waiting.
look.prompt: Which corner would draw the most riders in your town, and how could a design keep the two groups from crossing paths?

check.q: Where does the skatepark bowl come from?
choices: Backyard pools skaters rode during the 1976–77 California drought
check.why: Bowls grew from the empty backyard pools skaters rode during the drought of 1976–77.

check.q: What does a street plaza include?
choices: Only flat ground with nothing on it
Ledges, rails, manual pads, banks and short stairs
check.why: A plaza copies city features such as ledges, benches, rails, banks and stairs.

check.q: Why do many towns choose a hybrid park?
choices: It serves more styles and spreads riders out
It is always the smallest choice
check.why: Mixing street and transition areas draws different riders to different parts of the park.

lessons.title: Room for Beginners
lessons.mainIdea: A beginner area placed away from fast lines, with features that step up in size, lets new riders of any age learn safely.
reading: Every skilled skater started on a gentle bank. A park built only for advanced riders leaves out children, adults coming back after years, and anyone brand new. A *beginner area* with flat ground, low banks, a small quarter pipe and a low ledge lets people learn pushing, turning, kickturns and a first drop-in without dodging fast riders.

Placement matters as much as the features. Designers think about *lines*, the paths riders take through a park. If the beginner area sits where fast lines cross, collisions follow. Putting it to one side, with clear *sightlines* across it, keeps learners safer and lets parents watch from a bench.

Features can step up in size, such as a 0.6 m quarter pipe, then a 0.9 m one, then a 1.2 m one, so a rider moves up when the last size feels easy. The physics shows why this works: speed at the bottom grows with the square root of height, so doubling the height does not double the speed. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises that children under 5 should not ride skateboards and that children 6 to 10 should be supervised by an adult, so seating near the beginner area helps grown-ups do that job.

Programs fill a beginner area. Free lesson days, loaner boards and helmets, and quiet morning hours help people who feel nervous in a busy park. Asking beginners at the meetings what would bring them back is a quick way to learn what to build. Adults returning to skating often ask for the same things as children: gentle features, room to fall safely and a little space.

words.d: a part of a skatepark with small, gentle features set apart from fast riders
the paths riders take as they move through a skatepark from feature to feature
clear views across a space, so people can see each other and what is coming

look.title: Ramp Height and Speed at the Bottom
look.unit: m/s at the bottom, no friction
look.prompt: The 1.2 m ramp is twice as tall as the 0.6 m ramp. Is its speed twice as fast? Use the numbers to explain.

check.q: In skatepark design, what are lines?
choices: The rules posted at the gate
The paths riders take through the park
check.why: Lines are the routes riders follow from feature to feature.

check.q: Why should a beginner area sit to one side, away from fast lines?
choices: To keep new riders out of collisions and easy to watch
Because beginners need the steepest ramps
So no one can see it
check.why: Placing it away from fast lines, with clear sightlines, keeps learners safer and lets parents watch.

check.q: Doubling a ramp's height from 0.6 m to 1.2 m changes the predicted speed how?
choices: It raises it from about 3.4 to about 4.9 m/s
check.why: Speed grows with the square root of height, so 3.43 m/s becomes 4.85 m/s, not double.

lessons.title: Concrete, Steel and Wood
lessons.mainIdea: Poured concrete lasts longest and is quieter, while prefabricated ramps cost less to start but are louder and wear faster.
reading: Most permanent public parks are poured *concrete*. It lasts for decades and needs little upkeep beyond cleaning and patching. It is also quieter than hollow ramps, because there is no empty space under the surface to drum when wheels roll over it. Concrete costs the most up front and cannot be moved once it has set.

*Prefabricated* ramps are built in a factory from steel, wood or composite panels and set on a flat slab. They cost less to start and can be rearranged. They are louder, because the hollow frame booms like a drum, and their surfaces and fasteners wear and need replacing. Some towns start with prefabricated ramps to show that people will come, then build in concrete later.

The finish matters to the physics. Crews *trowel* concrete smooth so wheels roll with little resistance, and they shape each transition to a steady curve so a rider's path is predictable. A steel pipe along the top edge lets trucks grind smoothly. Ledges often get a metal edge so they stay square after thousands of grinds.

*Drainage* and shade belong in the design too. A flat bottom that holds puddles stays wet for days, and wet concrete is slippery and unsafe to ride. Slopes that carry water to drains, plus shade trees planted where their leaves will not fill a bowl, keep a park usable on more days of the year.

words.d: a building material of cement, sand, gravel and water that hardens like stone
built in pieces in a factory and put together at the site
to smooth wet concrete with a flat tool; also the name of the tool
the way water flows off a surface and away, so it does not pool

look.title: Two Parks After Five Years
look.text: Park A opened five years ago with steel and wood ramps on a slab. Its panels are scuffed, a few screws stick up, and neighbors hear a boom every time a rider lands. Park B opened the same year in poured concrete. Its surface has a few patched cracks, rainwater runs to a drain at the low corner, and the loudest sound is the click of trucks on coping.
look.prompt: If your town had only enough money for a small park, which would you choose first, and what would you tell the council about the long run?

check.q: Why is a concrete park usually quieter than a prefabricated one?
choices: There is no hollow space under the surface to drum
check.why: Hollow frames boom like a drum; solid concrete has no empty space underneath.

check.q: What is one advantage of prefabricated ramps?
choices: They cost less to start and can be moved
check.why: Factory-built ramps cost less up front and can be rearranged, though they are louder and wear faster.

check.q: Why does drainage matter in a skatepark?
choices: Puddles leave concrete wet and slippery for days
Drains are needed for the lights
It only matters for bowls indoors
check.why: Standing water makes concrete slippery and unsafe, so good slopes and drains keep a park rideable.

lessons.title: Girls and Women at the Park
lessons.mainIdea: Women have skated from the start, Olympic champions have raised their visibility, and simple design and programs help more girls and women ride.
reading: Women have skated since the sidewalk-surfing days. Patti McGee won the women's national title and appeared on the cover of Life magazine in 1965. Peggy Oki rode for the Zephyr team at the Del Mar Nationals in 1975. Even so, for decades many parks felt like places for boys, and girls often saw no one like them on the ramps.

The Olympics changed what many young riders see. At Tokyo 2020, held in 2021, 13-year-old Momiji Nishiya of Japan won women's street gold, and Rayssa Leal of Brazil, also 13, took silver. Sky Brown of Great Britain, 13, won bronze in park. At Paris 2024, Arisa Trew of Australia won women's park, and Coco Yoshizawa of Japan won women's street. That kind of *representation*, seeing people like yourself succeed, helps new riders picture themselves skating.

Planners can act on this. A weekly girls' and women's *skate night*, women coaches on lesson days, and a beginner area away from the busiest lines help new riders feel welcome. Good lighting, restrooms, seating and clear views across the park are simple features that help many riders feel safe.

*Inclusion* means planning so everyone can take part. Invite girls and women to design meetings directly, through schools, clubs and community groups, not only through skate shops. Their requests, such as a quieter learning space or programs at set times, often help beginners of every gender too.

words.d: seeing people like yourself in a role, such as an athlete, on a team or in the news
a set time at a park or rink reserved for a group, such as girls and women
planning a place or program so that everyone can take part and feel welcome

check.why: Inclusion means designing places and programs so everyone can join in.

lessons.title: Adaptive Riders and WCMX
lessons.mainIdea: Wheelchair and other adaptive riders use skateparks too, and smooth paths, step-free entries and gentle access ramps let them reach the features.
reading: Skateparks are not only for boards. In *WCMX*, short for wheelchair motocross, riders use sturdy wheelchairs on ramps and in bowls. Aaron Fotheringham, a pioneer of the sport, landed the first wheelchair backflip in the mid-2000s. His riding showed that quarter pipes and bowls work for wheelchairs as well as boards.

*Adaptive* skaters ride in ways that fit their bodies. Some sit on the board, some use a wheelchair, some skate with a prosthetic leg, and some are blind or have low vision and learn a park by sound and touch. Adaptive skate programs lend equipment and teach in small steps, as any good coach does.

A park that welcomes wheelchair riders needs a way in. A smooth, paved path from the sidewalk and parking lot, an *accessible* entrance with no steps, and gentle ramps up to the decks at the top of features let a rider reach the riding areas at all. Transitions with a steady curve, smooth flat bottoms and wide flat ground for turning suit wheelchairs well.

Ask adaptive riders to review the plans, and invite a WCMX rider or an adaptive program to a meeting. The same features that help them, such as gentle access ramps and smooth paths, also help parents with strollers, older visitors and beginners. Planning for access from the first drawing costs far less than adding it after the concrete sets.

words.d: wheelchair motocross: riding a sturdy wheelchair on skatepark ramps and bowls
changed to fit a rider's body or needs, as in adaptive skating or adaptive equipment
easy to reach and use for people of all abilities, including wheelchair users

look.title: Two Ways Into the Same Park
look.text: At Park A, the only way from the parking lot is a grass slope and three concrete steps, and the quarter pipe deck is reached by a short ladder. At Park B, a smooth path runs from the sidewalk to a wide gate, and a gentle ramp climbs to the deck of each quarter pipe. A WCMX rider arrives at both.
look.prompt: What would the rider be able to do at each park, and what would it cost to change Park A?

check.q: What is WCMX?
choices: Riding a wheelchair on skatepark ramps and bowls
check.why: WCMX means wheelchair motocross, riding sturdy wheelchairs in skateparks.

check.q: Who landed the first wheelchair backflip in the mid-2000s?
check.why: Aaron Fotheringham, a WCMX pioneer, landed the first wheelchair backflip in the mid-2000s.

check.q: Which feature most helps a wheelchair rider reach a park's features?
choices: A smooth path, a step-free entrance and gentle ramps to the decks
A tall fence with one narrow gate
check.why: Step-free paths and gentle access ramps let wheelchair riders get to the riding areas.

lessons.title: Safety, Lighting and Noise
lessons.mainIdea: Clear views, even lighting on a timer and distance from homes make a park safer and quieter, and sound drops about 6 decibels per doubling of distance.
reading: Safe parks are designed, not just posted. Signs typically ask riders to wear helmets and take turns, and list the hours. Open views across the park allow *passive supervision*, the everyday watching that happens when riders, parents and people walking by can see what is going on. A posted street address helps an ambulance find the park quickly.

Lighting adds hours, especially in winter, when it gets dark before many people finish school or work. LED lights on a timer that switches off at closing time can light the riding surfaces evenly without shining into nearby windows. Even light matters, because dark patches hide the cracks and stones that stop a wheel.

Noise is a common worry for neighbors, and physics helps answer it. Sound spreads out as it travels, so it gets quieter with distance. In open air, from a small source, each doubling of distance lowers the level by about 6 *decibels*. If wheels and tails measure 80 dB at 10 m in this worked example, the level is about 74 dB at 20 m, 68 dB at 40 m and 62 dB at 80 m.

Designers use that rule when they place a park. Setting the riding area farther from homes, choosing concrete over hollow ramps, and putting a *berm* or a building between the park and houses all cut noise. A sound meter, or a phone app as a rough guide, can record levels at the nearest home before and after, which gives the council real numbers.

words.d: the natural watching that happens when people nearby can easily see into a space
units (dB) for how loud a sound is; a few decibels lower sounds noticeably quieter
a low, wide bank of earth used to block sound or views

look.title: Sound Level and Distance
look.cite: Worked example: about 6 dB lower for each doubling of distance from a small source in open air
look.prompt: If the nearest home is 40 m from the park, what level does the example predict there? What would moving the park to 80 m do?

check.q: What is passive supervision?
choices: The natural watching that happens when people can see into a space
A rule that parents must stay home
check.why: Open views let riders, parents and passersby notice what is happening without a guard.

check.q: In open air, about how much does sound drop each time the distance doubles?
check.why: Spreading sound loses about 6 dB for each doubling of distance from a small source.

check.q: In the worked example, a park measures 80 dB at 10 m. About what level is it at 40 m?
check.why: Two doublings, 10 to 20 m and 20 to 40 m, each subtract about 6 dB: 80 − 12 = 68 dB.

lessons.title: Parks Skaters Built Themselves
lessons.mainIdea: Burnside, the Southbank undercroft and Skateistan show how skaters who build and care for a space can change how a city sees them.
reading: In 1990, skaters in Portland, Oregon, began pouring concrete under the Burnside Bridge without permission. It was a *DIY* park, short for do it yourself. They shaped banks and walls by hand, paid for supplies themselves and kept building. Over time the city accepted the park instead of tearing it out, and Burnside became one of the best-known skateparks in the world.

In London, skaters have ridden the *undercroft* beneath the Southbank Centre since the 1970s. When a redevelopment plan threatened to move them, the Long Live Southbank *campaign* gathered wide public support, and an agreement in 2014 kept the space for skating. The campaign treated a skate spot as part of the city's culture, worth saving like a theater or a gallery.

In 2007, Oliver Percovich founded Skateistan in Kabul, Afghanistan, starting with a few boards and children who gathered to ride. It grew into a skate school that paired skateboarding with classroom lessons, and it welcomed girls, who had few chances to play sport in public. It shows that a skate space can also be a place to learn.

These stories show a pattern useful to any proposal: skaters who show up, build trust and care for a space can change how a city sees them. They also show the limits. Building without permission carries real risks, so most towns now invite skaters into the official process, where the work is legal, inspected and built to last.

words.d: do it yourself; a skate spot built by skaters themselves, often without official help
a covered space beneath a building; at Southbank, the area skaters ride under the arts center

lessons.title: Writing the Proposal
lessons.mainIdea: A strong proposal answers the council's questions with evidence: need, site, design, cost, safety and support.
reading: A *proposal* is the written case for the park. A strong one fits on a few pages and answers the questions council members will ask. Why is a park needed? Where will it go, and what will it look like? What will it cost, and who will pay? How will it be kept safe and clean?

*Evidence* makes the case. Count how many people skate in town, with a survey at schools and a sign-in sheet at a skate-a-thon. List where skaters ride now and the problems that causes, such as tickets or close calls with cars in parking lots. Your own measurements help too: the slope of a proposed site from a 1-meter level test, or a sound reading at the nearest home.

Use examples from towns like yours. Find a nearby park of similar size, then ask its parks department how many people use it, what upkeep costs each year and what they would change. Facts from a real neighbor carry more weight than general claims. Attach the design drawings, the budget table and each *letter of support* from parents, teachers, police or local businesses.

Write plainly. Lead with a one-paragraph summary, use headings and put numbers in tables. Thank the people who helped. When the proposal goes to the council, bring skaters of different ages to speak briefly, so members can see the whole community the park would serve.

words.d: a written plan that asks decision-makers to approve and fund a project
facts and measurements that support a claim
a signed letter from a person or group saying why they back a project

look.title: A Proposal on One Page
look.text: Picture the first page. At the top, a three-sentence summary: 140 people skate in town, they now ride in parking lots, and a 1,200 m² park by the library would serve them. Below, five headings: Need, Site, Design, Budget, Safety and Upkeep. Under Need, a small table of survey results by school. At the bottom, a list of twelve letters of support.
look.prompt: What one piece of evidence would you collect first for a park in your town, and how would you measure it?

check.q: Which question should a skatepark proposal answer?
choices: Who is the best skater in town?
Which brand of board is best?
What will it cost, and who will pay?
check.why: Councils need to know the cost and the funding plan, along with need, site, design and safety.

check.q: Which is strong evidence of need for a park?
choices: A guess that many people might skate
A single opinion with no numbers
A school survey counting how many people skate
check.why: Counted results from a survey are facts the council can check.

check.q: Why compare with a nearby park of similar size?
choices: Facts from a real neighbor carry more weight than general claims
To prove your town is larger
Because the council requires it in every state
check.why: Real numbers on use and upkeep from a similar park make the case more believable.

review.q: Which step comes first in getting a public skatepark built?
choices: Advocates show there is a need
The park opens with rules posted
review.why: The process begins when advocates organize and show the city that people need a park.

review.q: Which part of a park comes from the backyard pools of the 1976–77 drought?
review.why: Bowls grew from the empty pools skaters rode during the California drought.

review.q: What is the main reason concrete parks are popular for permanent public sites?
choices: They are the cheapest to start
They can be moved each season
They last for decades with little upkeep and are quieter
review.why: Concrete lasts a long time, needs little care and makes less noise than hollow ramps.

review.q: In a budget, what is money set aside for surprises called?
review.why: A contingency is held back for unexpected costs.

review.q: Who founded Skateistan in Kabul in 2007?
review.why: Oliver Percovich founded Skateistan, a skate school in Kabul, in 2007.

review.q: Which design choice most helps wheelchair riders?
choices: Step-free entrances and gentle ramps to the decks
review.why: Step-free paths and gentle access ramps let wheelchair riders reach the features.

review.q: A park measures 74 dB at 20 m. Using the 6 dB rule, about what is the level at 40 m?
review.why: Doubling the distance from 20 m to 40 m lowers the level by about 6 dB: 74 − 6 = 68 dB.

review.q: What makes public comment at a council meeting most effective?
choices: A long speech with no facts
Skipping the meeting and emailing later
A short talk with who you are, what you ask for and a few facts
review.why: Brief, factual talks that state the request clearly help members decide.
